title: Classification

textbookText: Classification Class 1. Polychaeta (Gr; polys-many; chaite-hairs) i. Mostly marine and some are found in fresh water. ii. Distinct head with eyes, palps and tentacles. iii. Locomotary organs are fleshy lateral outgrowth called parapodia. iv. Clitellum is absent. v. Sexes are separate. vi. Fertilization is external, and presence of trochophore larva.
Example: Nereis (sand worm), Aphrodite (sea mouse), Glycera, Arenicola (lug worm) etc.

Class 2. Oligochaeta (Gr; oligos-few; chaite-hairs) i. Mostly terrestrial and some of them are found in freshwater. ii. Head is indistinct and without eyes and tentacles. iii. Locomotary organs are setae embedded in skin. No parapodia. iv. Presence of glandular clitellum that forms cocoon. v. Hermaphrodite and fertilization is external that takes place in cocoon. vi. Direct development i.e. no larval stages.
Example: Pheretima (Earthworm), tubifex (sludge worm), Lumbricus, Megascolex etc.

Class 3. Hirudinea i. They are both terrestrial and aquatic, mostly ectoparasitic or blood feeding (sanguivorous). ii. Body is elongated, dorsoventrally flattened or cylindrical. iii. Both anterior end and posterior end of the body bear suckers used to adhere on host skin and locomotion. (No parapodia and setae) iv. Coelom is greatly reduced and filled with botryoidal tissue and blood. v. Clitelum is developed temporarily only, during breeding season. vi. Body consists of usually 33 segments and each segment is further sub-divided superficially into annuli. vii. Hermaphrodite, internal fertilization and direct development.
Example: Hirudinaria (cattle leech), Piscicola (fish leech), Hirudo (medicinal leech), Haemopis etc.

Class 4. Archiannelida i. They are exclusively marine and primitive worms of about a dozen genera. ii. Body is small and elongated with distinct internal segmentation. External segmentation is fainted. iii. No parapodia or setae. iv. Sexes are usually separate and larval form is called trochophore. v. Prostomium bears 2 or 3 tentacles.
